title: Maryland high court strikes Dove from House ballot
summary: An Anne Arundel County Democrat is ineligible to run for the House of Delegates after the Supreme Court of Maryland on Monday affirmed a lower court ruling striking him from the ballot.
content:
by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters April 13, 2026

by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters April 13, 2026

An Anne Arundel County Democrat is ineligible to run for the House of Delegates after the Supreme Court of Maryland on Monday affirmed a lower court ruling striking him from the ballot.

John Dove Jr. claimed he changed his residence from Gambrills to Pasadena in order to challenge Del. Gary Simmons (D-Anne Arundel) in legislative District 12B. The Supreme Court of Maryland disagreed Monday afternoon, hours after hearing Dove’s appeal, issuing a one-page order affirming Anne Arundel County Circuit Court Judge Robert J. Thompson’s week-old decision.

“I’m grateful that the Supreme Court ruled in favor of our petition to remove Mr. Dove from the ballot,” Simmons said in a statement. “I’m glad to be able to bring this to a close to be able to focus on the general election.”

The order, with an opinion to follow, comes just a week before an April 20 deadline to certify the ballots.

The Maryland State Board of Elections struck Dove from its list of candidates for the district on Monday afternoon. Simmons stands as the lone candidate in the Democratic primary. He would face Blair L. Brannock, the sole Republican running in the district, in the November general election.

This is the second time in two weeks that the high court has issued a ruling on the case.

The court on March 30 ordered the challenge filed by Simmons be sent back to the lower court, after Thompson ruled Simmons’ challenge was not ripe because the Maryland Constitution gives a candidate six months from the election to move into the district. That six-month clock would have given Dove until May 3 to move to Pasadena.

Last week, Thompson held a hearing on the remanded case.

Thompson said after the hearing that Dove fell victim “to bad timing,” juggling various situations regarding possible renovations of a home in his new district and the one where he has lived for years. While it might have been Dove’s intent to move, Thompson said “he hasn’t perfected that.”

Tiffany Alston, a state delegate and Dove’s attorney, said Thompson erred in the decision. She said the ruling would allow Simmons to eliminate a potential challenger without a single vote being cast.

Following the hearing Monday, Alston told reporters she felt confident that the court would rule in her client’s favor, but that if the case did not go Dove’s way, they could file a motion for the Supreme Court of Maryland to reconsider today’s order. She said Dove may also have an appeal on “equal protection” grounds with the U.S. Supreme Court.

Alston was on the House floor for voting on the last day of the 90-day session and not immediately available for comment.

— This story was updated to include the state Board of Elections’ decision to strike Dove from the ballot.
